summary: This document registers the application/cms media type for use with Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) content types.

eli5.summary: A file needs a label saying what it is. This creates the official label for CMS secure data files.

questions: how to identify cms protected files
subtitle: The MIME type for secure cryptographic data files

tldr.problem: CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) is a standard way to package data with cryptographic protection like signatures and encryption, but there was no standard MIME type to identify these files in email and HTTP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7193 registers the media type application/cms with optional parameters to describe what type of CMS content is inside (encapsulatingContent and innerContent), allowing programs to know what they are dealing with.
tldr.outcome: Applications and mail systems can now correctly identify and handle CMS-protected content when it arrives as an attachment or over the web, using a standard registered MIME type.
tldr.outcomeLabel: Standard MIME type for CMS data

today: RFC 7193 is an Informational specification that registered the application/cms media type with IANA. It established two registries for encapsulating and inner content types that are still maintained by IANA and can be extended with new types through Expert Review.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
CMS (Cryptographic Message Syntax) is a standard format for wrapping data with cryptographic protection. Data can be signed (so the receiver knows who sent it and that it hasn't been changed), enveloped (encrypted so only the intended recipient can read it), or combined with other types of protection. CMS is used in many places: email systems, software updates, certificate management, and secure data exchange.

Before RFC 7193, there was no standard way to label a CMS file when it arrived in email or over the web. Previous S/MIME (Secure MIME) specifications had registered the type application/pkcs7-mime, but that was limited. RFC 7193 creates a new, more general media type application/cms that can describe all kinds of CMS content types and combinations, making it easier for applications to understand what they are receiving.
sections.eli5: When you get a secure file in email, the system needs to know what kind of protection it has. This creates a standard way to label those files so the right program can open them.

sections.title: CMS Content Types and Wrapping
sections.content:
CMS uses two kinds of content types: encapsulating content types that wrap around other content to protect it, and inner content types that are the actual data being protected. Encapsulating types include SignedData (adds a digital signature), EnvelopedData (encrypts), EncryptedData (applies encryption without the key agreement), CompressedData (compresses for efficiency), AuthData (adds authentication without necessarily hiding the data), and others. Inner types are what the encapsulation protects: the raw data, firmware packages, keys, certificates, or specialized protocol messages.

One piece of CMS-protected content might have multiple layers: for example, data compressed (CompressedData), then encrypted (EnvelopedData), then signed (SignedData). Each layer is another encapsulating type wrapping what came before. The media type registration needed to handle this nesting, where multiple content types can be involved in a single file.
sections.eli5: Secure files are like boxes inside boxes. The outer boxes are the security measures (locked, signed, etc.), and the inner box is the actual data. The label needs to say what's in all the boxes.

sections.title: The application/cms Media Type and Parameters
sections.content:
RFC 7193 defines the application/cms media type with two optional parameters: encapsulatingContent and innerContent. The encapsulatingContent parameter lists which protection or wrapping types are applied to the data (one or more of authData, signedData, envelopedData, encryptedData, compressedData, contentCollection, contentWithAttrs, authEnvelopedData, encryptedKeyPkg, digestData, or contentInfo). The innerContent parameter lists what the protected content actually contains (one or more of firmwarePackage, trustAnchorList, asymmetricKeyPackage, symmetricKeyPackage, and many specialized types like TAMP protocol messages and key receipts).

For example, a file might be labeled as Content-Type: application/cms; encapsulatingContent=signedData; innerContent=trustAnchorList to indicate it contains a signed list of trust anchors (trusted certificate authorities). This lets programs know immediately what to expect without having to parse the entire file structure.
sections.eli5: The label tells you what protection is on the file and what kind of data is inside, so the right tool knows how to open it.

sections.title: Registries of Encapsulating and Inner Content Types
sections.content:
RFC 7193 establishes two IANA registries: the CMS Encapsulating Content Types registry and the CMS Inner Content Types registry. The registries list all the standard types that can appear in the encapsulatingContent and innerContent parameters. Each entry includes the type name, the RFC that defines it, and the object identifier (OID) that uniquely identifies it in the ASN.1 encoding. New CMS content types are registered through Expert Review, meaning the IANA expert checks whether a new type is truly an encapsulating type (it wraps something) or an inner type (something is wrapped around it).

For example, RFC 5652 defines SignedData, EnvelopedData, and other CMS content types. RFC 4108 defines firmware package types. RFC 5934 defines TAMP (Trust Anchor Management Protocol) message types. All of these are listed in the registries so that new applications and future protocols can reference them consistently.
sections.eli5: There are official lists of all the different ways data can be protected and all the different kinds of data that can be protected. New security methods have to be added to the official list.

sections.title: How This Improves Interoperability
sections.content:
Before RFC 7193, when an application received a CMS-protected file, it often had to examine the structure to figure out what was inside. With the media type and parameters clearly labeled, a receiver can immediately understand what protections are applied and what kind of content to expect. This is especially important for protocols that need to handle CMS content in many different combinations, such as CMC (Certificate Management over CMS) or other protocols built on CMS foundations.

The RFC also clarifies that all CMS content types are wrapped in a ContentInfo structure as the outermost layer, per RFC 5652. This is important for interoperability: both sender and receiver know that the actual CMS structure starts with ContentInfo. Applications using the application/cms media type should include both the encapsulatingContent and innerContent parameters when sending files so receivers have maximum information about what they are dealing with.
sections.eli5: When both the sender and receiver know what the labels mean, they can work with each other automatically without needing special translation or manual setup.
